sentences.text: The type species of the genus Compsognathus is Compsognathus longipes, a name established by Johann A. Wagner in 1859.
While members of this species were once thought to reach the size of a chicken, the German specimen is now believed to be a juvenile, which explains its small stature.
The German individual stood about 70 to 75 centimeters tall and measured 89 centimeters in length, weighing between 0.32 and 0.58 kilograms.
In contrast, the French specimen was larger, estimated at 1.25 meters tall and 1.4 meters long, with a weight ranging from 2.5 to 3.5 kilograms.
This predator possessed small, pointed teeth suited for eating small vertebrates, a diet confirmed by lizard remains found in the stomach of the German specimen.
Although the genus was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1875, it was first described by Johann A. Wagner in 1859.
Later, Bidar and colleagues named Compsognathus corallestris in 1972, but it is now considered a synonym of Compsognathus longipes.
A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and colleagues examined nine foot bones for stress fractures but found none.
The French specimen contained unidentified lizards or sphenodontids in its stomach, further evidence of its carnivorous nature.
Friedrich von Huene erected the infraorder Coelurosauria in 1914, which includes the family Compsognathidae, the group to which Compsognathus belongs.
The deposits containing the German specimen date to the latest Kimmeridgian or earlier Tithonian stages, when the region was part of the Solnhofen archipelago.
The French specimen dates to the lower Tithonian based on ammonite index fossils.
Jens Zinke assigned forty-nine teeth from the Guimarota coal mine to Compsognathus sp. in 1998, noting they differ from C. longipes teeth due to serrations on the front edge.
The number of digits on the hand of Compsognathus remains a subject of scientific debate.
A 2022 review interprets the tail skin impressions as aberrant bony growths rather than scales because they are texturally and mineralogically indistinguishable from the vertebrae.
Bidar and colleagues argued in 1972 that the French specimen had webbed hands that would have looked like flippers in life.
